---
title: "Neuroplastic Turn"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-02-13"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

The canonical explanation of depression was so-called the monoamine hypothesis, which posits that depression is caused by a deficiency in monoamine neurotransmitters and that increasing the concentrations of these molecules would produce therapeutic effects [@SCHILDKRAUT1965]. However, the fatal weakness of this model is that it cannot explain the delayed onset of treatment response. This explanatory gap prompted a paradigm shift toward a neuroplasticity hypothesis.

The newer hypothesis proposed that chronic stress reduces the expression of BDNF in limbic structures, leading to synaptic atrophy and neuronal loss. Conversely, antidepressant treatment upregulates BDNF and TrkB, thereby promoting neurogenesis and neuronal survival [@duman1999]. Key evidence for this hypothesis included findings that chronic antidepressant exposure increases hippocampal neurogenesis [@Malberg2000] and that blocking this process prevents behavioral effects in preclinical models [@Santarelli2003].

The delayed response of antidepressants was explained that critical therapeutic events occur downstream of neurotransmitter receptor binding. During this delay, intracellular signal transduction triggers gene transcription and de novo protein synthesis that support the neurons' intrinsic functions. Ultimately, these intrinsic functions manifest as structural and functional plasticity, involving the strengthening or weakening of existing synapses and the formation of new synaptic connections [@Castrn2013; @Casarotto2021].

Rapid-acting antidepressants, such as ketamine and psychedelics, further accelerated this neuroplastic turn. Unlike traditional agents, these substances induce therapeutic effects with remarkable speed, bypassing the weeks-long delay typical of monoaminergic drugs. Ketamine’s efficacy has been linked to rapid, mTOR-dependent synaptogenesis [@Li2010], while psychedelics appear to trigger massive cortical desynchronization followed by robust structural and functional remodeling [@Ly2018; @Shao2021]. ECT has undergone a similar conceptual evolution. While early models focused on acute neurotransmitter surges or anticonvulsant properties, contemporary perspectives view ECT as a primary driver of multi-level plasticity, creating a permissive state for further circuit-level reorganization [@Nibuya1995; @Cano2023; @Laroy2025].
